segments.text: The campaign, I've got to say, picked a really lovely family to get this. Kyle, the son, is 41. He'd applied for this Freedom Dividend on behalf of his mom. About four years ago, the family lost Kyle's dad, Merle, to brain cancer. They seemed like such a tight, loving family.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Merle was a musician. And in their house, every Wednesday, it was music night. They'd play records-- Kiss, Black Sabbath. Merle would play drums, and the kids would dance around, which is how, I suppose, Kyle ended up being a musician, too.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Anyway, about a year after Merle died, Pam was also diagnosed with cancer. The day she was diagnosed-- her birthday-- her boss called her to tell her he was firing her because she'd had to miss too much work. Pam worked as an aide for disabled adults, which she said was hard, but she loved it.

segments.text: After that, Kyle dedicated himself to taking care of Pam. And Pam, now in remission, still has a hard time getting around. Kyle's been piecing together work-- auto repair, computer repair, music work when he can get it. But it's hard making sure he's there for his mom.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: The monthly bills are about $1,300, and they barely get covered. So $1,000 would mean a lot. Kyle, though, he says he'd like to see his mom spend at least some of this imaginary money, even just a little, on something genuinely frivolous.

segments.speaker: Kyle Christiansen
segments.text: Yeah, I'd just like to see her just go buy something because she wants to and not out of necessity.

segments.speaker: Pam Christiansen
segments.text: But there's priorities, too, so.

segments.speaker: Kyle Christiansen

segments.text: Yeah, I know for me, I used to have a full-blown recording studio here in town. And I've always kind of held on to all that equipment hoping to set one up somewhere. segments.speaker: Pam Christiansen
segments.text: Oh!

segments.text: So congratulations.

segments.speaker: Pam Christiansen
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.text: If Yang did this for everyone, if he gave every adult $12,000 a year, it would cost the government $2 trillion, give or take. The current federal budget is $4 trillion. Yang has projections on how all this could be paid for, and they include some very optimistic assumptions, all for a theory that's never been tested on anywhere near the scale.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Yang starts to explain to the Christiansens how this is going to work for them. But mostly, he tells them how grateful he is to help them out, in a way that feels pretty nice, actually. And it kind of drains a little awkwardness out of a very manufactured situation.

segments.speaker: Andrew Yang
segments.text: So we need to do this for people all over the country, but starting here with you all to illustrate the fact that if people get some extra money in their hands, it's going to go to the things that we care about and value. segments.speaker: Pam Christiansen
segments.text: Thank you. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Andrew Yang
segments.text: You guys are very, very welcome.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: The next 45 minutes are completely usual and unusual. Yang genuinely asks Pam and Kyle about their situation-- Pam's neuropathy, her treatment. He talks again and again about how much he admires Kyle for taking care of his mom. Kyle talks about the one doctor's appointment he's missed in the last three years. They talk about music, how Kyle quit the metal band he was touring with because he loved performing, but he never had an interest in the drinking and drugs that went with it. They laugh about Yang's flag socks. He talks about picking them out.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Like so little of political campaigning, it's unrushed enough to feel regular. Until it's time to go and the surreal logistics of a political campaign break through this small bubble of normality. Yang has to hit the road.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I feel like this is a weird and particular thing you see when politicians campaign. So many of their interactions are superficial and crassly abbreviated. And then sometimes, like in this room, they'll just drift into a space with some voters that feels intense, and authentic, and personal. And then poof, time to go.

segments.text: And this one guy was wiping tears away. At this point, Weigel can sort of divide the candidates into two groups. And it's not the moderates and the far left. segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And for our last story, we are joined now by one of our producers, David Kestenbaum. Hey, David.

segments.speaker: Sarah Longwell
segments.text: No, I mean, I was just up in Manchester, and I did a series of focus groups. If you ask them specifically, hey, would you be open to an alternative in 2020? And then for other people, it's just an openness, like a willingness for political competition.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: One thing that really surprises people in these focus groups, she says, is when you explain just how much the debt has gone up under Trump. It's increased more during the first two years of Trump than it did the previous two years under Obama.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Bill Kristol lays out how this all might go for a challenger. You raise a little money, go to Iowa, New Hampshire. Maybe you get 30% of the vote in New Hampshire. That is a serious blow to the president. You're off and running. So that's their case.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: There is one kind of noticeable challenge to this plan. Since we've had the current primary system, there are zero examples-- zero-- of someone challenging a sitting president in a primary and actually winning.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I mean, is some part of this just kind of like theater? And I mean theater you truly believe in?

segments.speaker: Bill Kristol
segments.text: I mean, I don't want to say yes because of course-- because that really isn't. I don't think of it that way. I'm not a very theatrical person. And I don't want to simply leave that stage on the Republican side alone to Donald Trump.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I'm still trying to think through just, like in your mind, why you're doing this. And is part of it just like a feeling like what is democracy for, if I can't cast a vote for the person I really want to be in office?

segments.speaker: Bill Kristol
segments.text: Yeah, I think it's actually people are overthinking this. I mean, I'm doing it because I don't think Trump should have a second term. I'm a Republican. But maybe because they damaged the president, he does not win re-election. In other words, this may be the bargain. You can run for president, possibly shape history, end Trump, change who wins, but you don't get to win.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I mean, it's interesting. The other Republicans I talked to pointed out that history is not on your side. segments.speaker: Bill Kristol
segments.text: No, but I think it's also holding out an alternative in a good way. But yeah--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Or sabotage. I mean--

segments.speaker: Bill Kristol
segments.text: Well, people can say that. They said that about the French who didn't go along with Vichy. I mean, what are you supposed to do? If you think it's bad--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I love that every time I have a point that's historical--

segments.speaker: Bill Kristol
segments.text: If you think it's bad for the country, they can say it's sabotage. I would say it's opposition. I don't think it's sabotage. Sabotage implies secrecy and deception. I don't think there's a heck of a lot of secrecy and deception in what I'm doing. I think I've been pretty open about my opposition, so I feel like I'm-- isn't that the point of America?

segments.speaker: Bill Kristol
segments.text: Honestly, if I were a Democrat, I would call me up and say, here's a lot of money for a primary challenge-- and we have talked to a lot of Democrats about this, obviously-- against Donald Trump. But we don't know which of those will actually be a good nominee against Trump. segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Wait, but is your goal to run somebody who's going to win the nomination and maybe the presidency? Or is your goal just to take down Trump?
